sub_title  
# GRADIENT DESCENT - LEARNING RATE 

 text  
- Neg. gradient is direction that looks locally promising to reduce \(R_{\text{emp}}\). 

 text  
- Hence weights components higher in which \(R_{\text{emp}}\) decreases more. 

 text  
- However, the length of \(-\frac{d}{d\theta} R_{\text{emp}}\) measures only the local decrease rate, i.e., there are no guarantees that we will not go "too far".

## ENCODING FOR CATEGORICALS  

 text  
We expand the representation of a variable \(x\) with \(k\) mutually exclusive categories from a scalar to a length- \(\bar{k}\) vector with at most one element being 1, and 0 otherwise: \(\pmb {\sigma}(x)_j = \mathbb{I}(x = j)\in \{0,1\}\)  

 text  
Each entry of \(\pmb {\sigma}(x)\in \{0,1\}^{\bar{k}}\) is treated as a separate feature.  

 text  
Two popular ways to do this are  

 text  
One- hot encoding: \(\bar{k} = k\) dummies, so exactly one element is 1 ("hot"). E.g. \(\left(x\in \{a,b,c\}\right)\mapsto \pmb {\sigma}(x) = (x_a,x_b,x_c)\) , with \(x_{a} = x_{b} = 0,x_{c} = 1\) and \(\pmb {\sigma}(x)\coloneqq (0,0,1)\) for \(x = c\)  

 text  
Dummy encoding: \(\bar{k} = k - 1\) dummies, so at most one element is 1, removing the redundancy of one- hot encoding (necessary for learners that require non- singular input matrices, such as in linear regression).  

 text  
E.g., \(x\in \{a,b,c\} \mapsto \pmb {\sigma}(x) = (x_a,x_b)\) for reference category \(c\) , with \(x_{a} = x_{b} = 0\) and \(\pmb {\sigma}(x) = (0,0)\) for \(x = c\)  

 text  
We also often use this encoding for categorical targets.  

 text  
For features with a natural order in their categories we resort to encodings that reflect this ordinality, e.g., a sequence of integer values.
